text: Every trading day, markets move. Prices jump, interest rates shift, currencies swing, and somewhere a portfolio quietly loses value. In 2008, and again in 2020, firms that understood their market risk survived, and many that didn't, failed. The people who measure that risk, model it, and keep it within limits are among the most sought-after professionals in finance. This course is how you become one of them.

Welcome to Market Risk Modeling, from RiskHub. Over sixteen modules, you'll go from the foundations of market risk to the models banks use every day: sensitivities, value at risk, expected shortfall, stress testing, backtesting, and regulatory capital. You'll apply it all in hands-on capstone projects, and you'll finish with a Certificate of Completion.

You'll learn from two practitioners who have done this work. Prateek Yadav is the C-E-O of RiskHub. He is an F-R-M and C-Q-F charterholder, has worked at J.P. Morgan, E-Y, and P-W-C, and is an alumnus of I-I-T Kanpur. Sudhanshu Kanwar is an instructor at RiskHub. He holds the F-R-M, C-F-A, and C-Q-F, has worked at Goldman Sachs and HSBC, and is an alumnus of I-I-M Ahmedabad.

The sixteen modules build on each other in four parts. First, the foundations and the risk factors. Then, risk modeling across rates, volatility, and every major asset class. Then, how risk is measured and aggregated. And finally, how models are tested, validated, and governed. Each module combines the intuition, the mathematics, and hands-on practice in Python, so you don't just understand the models, you can build them.

Module one, Foundations of Market Risk. You'll begin by defining market risk and how it's measured. Then you'll see how market risk differs from credit, liquidity, and operational risk. Next, you'll explore the trading book, the banking book, and real-world context. Finally, you'll learn how to choose a market risk measure, and how to test it.

Module two, Types and Classification of Market Risk Exposure. Start with the four standard market-risk classes: interest rate, equity, foreign exchange, and commodity. Then go further, into credit spread risk and volatility risk. You'll study basis risk, and the difference between directional and relative-value exposure. And you'll learn to decompose multi-leg trades into the individual exposures.

Module three, Risk Factors and Sensitivities. First, the foundations of risk factors. Then, what a sensitivity really means, and how to measure it. You'll study curvature, approximation error, and how to map positions onto risk factors. And you'll finish with the sensitivities required under FRTB, and the most common points of confusion.

Module four, Interest Rate Risk Modeling. Start with yield curve fundamentals. Then measure price risk with duration and convexity. Move on to key rate durations and curve risk. And finish with interest rate derivatives, and the term structure models used to price and simulate them.

Module five, Volatility and Options Risk, and the Greeks. Lay the foundations of option pricing. Then measure how an option's value reacts to the underlying with delta and gamma. Add vega, theta, and rho, for volatility, time, and interest rates. And finish with volatility surfaces, the smile, and skew.

Module six, Value at Risk, Parametric and Historical. Begin with VaR foundations and precise definitions: the loss you won't exceed on ninety-nine days out of a hundred. Then compute it with the parametric, variance-covariance method. Next, calculate it again using historical simulation. And close by examining VaR's limitations, and comparing the methods side by side.

Module seven, Monte Carlo Simulations and Advanced VaR. Learn the foundations of Monte Carlo simulation. Then implement Monte Carlo VaR, step by step, in Python. Make it faster and more accurate with variance reduction techniques. And apply simulation to complex portfolios, full of options and non-linear positions.

Module eight, Expected Shortfall and Tail Risk. Go beyond VaR with coherent risk measures, and see why VaR isn't one. Then learn the fundamentals of expected shortfall, the measure that tells you how bad the tail really gets. Study extreme value theory. And finish with fat tails and tail dependence, when assets crash together.

Module nine, Fixed Income Risk Modeling. Start with fixed income instruments and the risk factors that drive them. Then compute VaR for a bond portfolio using full revaluation. Next, use partial revaluation and sensitivity-based VaR. And finally, compare partial and full revaluation in practice: where the shortcut works, and where it breaks down.

Module ten, Equity Risk Modeling. Cover the fundamentals of equity risk. Then measure systematic risk with beta, factor models, and the capital asset pricing model. Study equity volatility and correlation, and how both change when markets fall. And finish with the risk of equity derivatives.

Module eleven, Foreign Exchange Risk Modeling. Learn how F-X markets work. Then identify the different types of F-X exposure a firm carries: transaction, translation, and economic. Design F-X hedging strategies that match those exposures. And finish with F-X derivatives, and cross-currency risk across a global portfolio.

Module twelve, Commodity Risk Modeling. Start with commodity market fundamentals: energy, metals, and agriculture. Then read futures curves and basis, including contango and backwardation. Model commodity volatility and seasonality, from winter gas spikes to harvest cycles. And finish with the risk of commodity derivatives.

Module thirteen, Correlation, Covariance, and Portfolio Aggregation. Build the fundamentals of correlation and covariance. Then estimate covariance matrices that hold up in practice. Aggregate VaR across a portfolio, and measure the diversification benefit. And finish with copulas and dependence modeling, for when simple correlation isn't enough.

Module fourteen, Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis. Learn stress testing fundamentals. Then replay history with historical scenarios, like the 2008 crisis and the 2020 COVID shock. Design hypothetical and reverse stress tests to find what would break the portfolio. And finish with the regulatory stress testing frameworks that banks are required to follow.

Module fifteen, Backtesting and Model Validation. Start with backtesting fundamentals: comparing VaR against actual P and L, and counting exceptions. Then apply the statistical tests, like Kupiec, Christoffersen, and the Basel traffic light, that decide whether a model passes. Learn the model validation frameworks used by banks and regulators. And finish with model risk management.

Module sixteen, Regulatory Capital and Governance, Basel and FRTB. Trace how the Basel framework evolved. Then work through the FRTB standardised approach, and the internal models approach, with its expected shortfall capital. And finish with risk governance, limits, and reporting: how it all comes together inside a bank.

Then you put it all together in two capstone projects. Each one is a full model validation, done the way a bank's independent validation team would do it. In the first, you validate an interest rate swap pricing model. You'll set out the swap, the curves, and the valuation framework, independently replicate and benchmark the price, test the model's sensitivities and stress outcomes, and deliver your findings, remediation, and validation decision. In the second, you validate a historical VaR model. You'll document the portfolio, the risk factors, and the VaR engine, independently replicate the VaR calculation, test the model with backtesting, stress, and attribution, and deliver your findings, the capital impact, and the validation decision.
Complete the modules and the capstone projects, and you'll earn a RiskHub Certificate of Completion in Market Risk Modeling, ready to add to your resume and your LinkedIn profile.

These skills lead to real roles. Market risk analysts, model validation analysts, quantitative risk analysts, F-R-T-B and regulatory capital specialists, and market risk managers. In India, indicative pay runs from about eight lakh a year at entry level to sixty lakh or more for senior managers. In the United States, from roughly seventy-five thousand dollars to over two hundred and fifty thousand. Actual pay depends on the firm, the city, and your experience.
